lead: A stepper motor moves in fixed angular steps when pulses arrive, so a controller can count steps instead of measuring position. A servo motor closes a feedback loop around a normal motor, so it corrects any error between commanded and actual position. A brushless DC (BLDC) motor uses an inverter to switch stator coils in step with a permanent-magnet rotor, so it avoids brushes. These machines trade the simplicity of a plain DC motor for precise control in printers, robot arms and e-rickshaws.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.4 for torque and commutation, Chapter 3.6 for the universal motor, and Chapter 3.7 for fixed-speed synchronous behaviour.

sections.h3: Stepper motor: fixed steps in open loop

blocks.text: A stepper motor has a stator with m phase windings and a rotor with N<sub>r</sub> teeth. The controller energises the phases in sequence, so the rotor jumps from one aligned position to the next. Each jump is one step. The step angle β is the angle moved per step:

blocks.where: β is the step angle in degrees per step; m is the number of phases; N<sub>r</sub> is the number of rotor teeth.

blocks.text: The number of steps per revolution is 360° ÷ β, which equals m × N<sub>r</sub>. Position is open loop: the driver counts pulses from a known start. Pull-out torque is the largest torque the motor can carry at a given stepping rate without losing synchronism (losing steps). No sensor is needed if the load never exceeds the pull-out torque. Holding torque is the torque available with the windings energised and the shaft stationary. It needs current; with the current off, the motor does not hold the rated load. Speed depends on the pulse rate f<sub>p</sub>: speed = β × f<sub>p</sub>. Here β is in degrees per step, f<sub>p</sub> is in pulses per second, and speed is in degrees per second. Divide degrees per second by 6 to get rpm.

items: 3D printer axes and filament feed: a 1.8° motor moves a known distance by counting pulses.
CNC table and scanner: open-loop position control from a pulse train.
Only a few syllabi teach stepper driver circuits; switching and pulse generation details belong to Units 4 and 5.

sections.h3: Servo motor: feedback corrects the error

blocks.text: A servo motor is not one motor type. It is a DC or AC motor plus a position or speed sensor and a controller. The controller compares the command with the measured value and drives the motor to reduce the error. This is closed-loop control. A potentiometer, encoder or Hall sensor gives position. The error is e = θ<sub>cmd</sub> − θ<sub>act</sub>, where θ<sub>cmd</sub> is the commanded angle and θ<sub>act</sub> is the actual angle, both in degrees. The controller output is a voltage or current command to the motor drive.

If θact is too small, the drive increases torque in the forward direction; if θact is too large, the drive applies torque in the reverse direction. In a DC servo, the motor is a normal DC motor from Chapter 3.4; the commutator and brushes still exist. In an AC servo, an inverter drives a synchronous or induction motor. The sensor is what makes the machine a servo, not a special winding.

items: Robot arm joint: holds an angle under changing load.
CNC axis: follows a position command along a path.
Rudder or camera gimbal: rejects wind disturbance.

sections.h3: BLDC motor: brushes replaced by electronics

blocks.text: A BLDC motor has a permanent-magnet rotor and a stator with phase windings. There is no commutator. An inverter switches the stator phases in a sequence. The sequence must follow the rotor position, measured by Hall sensors or estimated from back EMF. This is electronic commutation. The inverter applies DC in blocks to two phases at a time. The current pattern makes a stator field that jumps in steps, and the magnet rotor follows the nearest stable alignment.

Because the switching is done by semiconductors, there are no brush sparks and no brush wear. Efficiency is high, life is long, and speed is set by the DC voltage the inverter applies to the windings and by the load; the commutation (switching) frequency follows the rotor position, so it is a result of the speed, not its setting. A PMSM is the sinusoidally driven cousin of the BLDC: it uses smoother three-phase currents and is often chosen for quiet, low-torque-ripple drives.

items: Ceiling fan: low-speed BLDC with a small inverter.
E-rickshaw: BLDC hub motor with battery and controller.
Drone: BLDC with an electronic speed controller.

figure.caption: Three families of special machines, each with one common use: the stepper runs open loop at 1.8° per step, the servo closes the loop with feedback, and the BLDC uses an inverter drive with no brushes.

spec.aria: A tree splits special machines into three families: stepper with 1.8 degrees per step in open loop driving a 3D printer, servo with feedback driving a robot arm, and BLDC with an inverter drive and no brushes driving a ceiling fan.

examples.question: A stepper motor has 4 phases and a rotor with 50 teeth. Find the step angle and the number of steps per revolution. How many pulses move the shaft through 90°, and what is the speed at 300 pulses per second? Give the speed in degrees per second and in rpm.
steps: Steps per revolution = 360° ÷ β = 360° ÷ 1.8° = 200 steps. Also m × N<sub>r</sub> = 4 × 50 = 200.
In rpm: 540°/s ÷ 6 = 90 rpm, because 360°/s equals 60 rpm.
examples.answer: β = 1.8°, 200 steps per revolution, 50 pulses for 90°, and 540°/s = 90 rpm at 300 pulses per second.
examples.check:
m = 4
Nr = 50
beta = 360 / (m * Nr)
steps = 360 / beta
pulses = 90 / beta
f = 300
speed = beta * f
rpm = speed / 6
print(beta)
print(int(steps))
print(int(pulses))
print(speed)
print(rpm)

traps: Step angle is not steps per revolution. β = 1.8° gives 200 steps per revolution; 200 is not the step angle.
A stepper does not hold its rated load with power removed. Holding torque needs current in the windings; permanent-magnet detent torque is much smaller.
Open-loop counting fails if the load torque exceeds the pull-out torque. The motor loses steps and the controller does not know.
A servo is a complete drive system, not a special motor winding. The motor inside can be a DC motor with brushes.
BLDC and PMSM are not identical in drive. BLDC usually uses block commutation; PMSM uses sinusoidal currents.

quiz.q: Define step angle and write its formula.
quiz.a: Step angle β is the angle moved by the rotor in one step. β = 360° ÷ (m × N<sub>r</sub>), where m is the number of phases and N<sub>r</sub> is the number of rotor teeth.

quiz.q: Why does a stepper motor need current in its windings to hold a load?
quiz.a: Holding torque comes from the magnetic field produced by winding current. With current off, only weak permanent-magnet detent torque remains, which is not the rated holding torque.

quiz.q: A 3-phase stepper motor has 40 rotor teeth. Find the step angle, the steps per revolution, and the pulses needed for 45°.
quiz.a: β = 360° ÷ (3 × 40) = 3° per step. Steps per revolution = 360° ÷ 3° = 120. Pulses for 45° = 45° ÷ 3° = 15 pulses.

quiz.q: A stepper in a 3D printer loses position after a jam clears. Give one likely cause and one fix.
quiz.a: The jam increased load torque beyond the pull-out torque, so the motor lost steps in open loop. Fix: reduce acceleration or increase current within rating, and home the axis with a sensor after a jam.

quiz.q: State one difference between a BLDC motor and a brushed DC motor.
quiz.a: A BLDC motor has no brushes or commutator; an inverter switches stator phases using rotor position. A brushed DC motor uses a mechanical commutator and brushes.

quiz.q: Why does a servo motor need a sensor?
quiz.a: The controller must know the actual position or speed to compute the error e = θ<sub>cmd</sub> − θ<sub>act</sub>. Without a sensor, it cannot correct the error.

quiz.q: A 1.8° stepper receives 400 pulses per second. Find its speed in degrees per second and in rpm.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses these machines in e-rickshaw controllers, drone electronic speed controllers, BLDC ceiling fans, robot servo drives and electric-vehicle traction motors. Research topics include field-oriented control for PMSM drives, sensorless rotor-position estimation, microstepping for quiet steppers, and servo tuning for fast settling. Search next for BLDC six-step commutation, field-oriented control, stepper microstepping and servo position control.
